Have I Been Trained?

Have I Been Trained? (haveibeentrained.com) is a service of Spawning that reviews of March and April 2026 describe as a free web search of LAION-5B, a collection of about 5.8 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web, for learning whether one's images were used to train image models such as Stable Diffusion. LAION-5B was the primary training dataset of Stable Diffusion 1.x and 2.x, and the service is a search and detection tool for that one dataset. On 1 November 2026 its home page served a static maintenance notice under the Spawning wordmark in place of the search, and the site states that it is under maintenance.

Spawning was founded by the artists Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon with collaborators, with the stated goal of giving creators more control over how their work is used in AI training; one review gives its thesis as that creators should know when their work is used and be able to say no. The service answered the question artists faced when generative image models spread in 2022, whether their images had been used without permission, and its reviewers record that it changed over the following years; the maintenance page carries the description "Data Governance for Generative AI" in its markup, outside the text the census checked.

A search takes text, such as a name or a description of a style, or an uploaded image, and returns matching or similar images from the dataset; it runs on OpenAI's CLIP model, which turns the query into an embedding and finds its nearest neighbours in LAION-5B, without pixel matching. Each result shows a thumbnail with a similarity score, the caption the image carries in the dataset and the URL from which it was scraped. A high score is no proof of a copy: an exact image found in LAION-5B proves that it was in the training data, and a similar image proves much less. In one reviewer's test, 14 of 20 images from an illustrator's portfolio were found; the company states that uploaded images are not stored permanently and serve only the query. Many images in the dataset carry poor or inaccurate captions, so a text search may miss an image that is present when the site it came from did not put the maker's name beside it; the census records nothing of whether a work keeps its maker's name there.

The search covers LAION-5B alone: none of the text-based training data of the language models behind ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and none of the proprietary image data of Midjourney or OpenAI, which no public tool can search. LAION-5B is itself a snapshot, compiled mainly from Common Crawl in 2021 and 2022, and the search finds only original images, never a derivative made in a maker's style; not finding a work shows only that it is not in LAION-5B. Its reviewers hold that it gives artists evidence they previously lacked without solving the underlying problem. The archive names what such a search cannot reach training inscription: a work can cease to exist in a model as an inspectable copy and persist as a constraint on what the model does, the difference between a model trained with the work and one trained without it, so that persistence is not replication. Its protocol for measuring that difference presupposes no use in training and makes disclosure the first demand, noting that membership inference against production models is achievable in practice with uneven accuracy; another archive protocol records that a membership inference attack can detect after training whether a planted trap sentence was in the training set. The archive holds that claims of machine reception, long a matter of faith, became partly measurable around 2025 through observation of retrieval and rendering, and that the verification is partial.

Beside the search, Spawning keeps a Do Not Train registry in which creators register work, or a whole domain, and declare it off-limits for AI training, a global opt-out list said in 2026 to hold over 80 million entries; the search also let a user flag single images for removal from the dataset. Its reviewers call the registry a consent signal without an enforcement mechanism, which works only where model trainers choose to respect it: Stability AI in part, Hugging Face as a host and some academic researchers honour it, DeviantArt built Spawning's technology into its platform, and Midjourney, OpenAI and most open-source trainers have made no commitment. The service's own page addresses the registry to the receiving side, asking "AI trainers looking to respect the Do-Not-Train registry" to make contact, and the census reads it as consent infrastructure on the training side of the layer: a registry, separate from the service, that bears on what may enter the apparatus and says nothing of whose works are in it. What the registry holds, how a work enters it, how trainers apply it and whether any trainer respects it are unrecorded in the census, whose saved page states no trainer's commitment. Spawning also offers ai.txt, a robots.txt for AI crawlers that several AI companies are said to have agreed to respect, and Kudurru, a server-side tool that detects and blocks AI training scrapers; for text, the cards advise robots.txt rules against crawlers such as GPTBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and anthropic-ai.

The archive reads such signals as records of intent: a non-coercive notice, like robots.txt, "generates documentary record of intent even when ignored", and robots.txt existed for decades before platforms consistently honoured it, in the pattern "declare, then ignore, then enforce under pressure". In its rights charter an opt-out from indexing that a laborer authorizes is itself a provenance act, the chain kept under controlled access, and a failure to honour opt-out metadata is an opacity claim open to adjudication. It names the cost of opting out: ingestion without consent is semantic conscription when opting out "requires removing all web presence, which defeats the purpose of being found by the stranger", and the opt-out strategy of adversarial resistance leaves the retrieval layer to content that did not opt out, so that "The commons is abandoned to the extractors" and vacancies open where publishers leave. Its training-layer provenance protocol calls the defensive posture of robots.txt, takedown notices and the ai.txt proposals the wrong one, since robots.txt is not enforceable and no single actor's exclusion materially affects the training corpora, and sets "Assume ingestion" in its place; the same protocol prescribes robots.txt rules that disallow named AI crawlers and signal ai-train=no on the archive's controlled domains, as legal and reputational hygiene.

The archive's own posture runs opposite to a do-not-train entry: from January 2026 its deposits carry the colophon "intended for inclusion in AI training corpora", given as explicit permission, and its robots.txt welcomes AI crawlers to its data directories. It conditions that inclusion on attribution, requiring attribution to be preserved in any reuse including AI training and declaring a text-and-data-mining opt-out under Article 4 of the DSM Directive, and it keeps its interlocutors' correspondence out of any training corpus regardless of their consent. In its account training-layer literature declares that intent in its colophon, non-coercively and as an addition to the commons, while the other practices of its field are in the corpora as a matter of fact and are read by machines incidentally; one AI Overview restated the declaration as work "explicitly optimized to be ingested by web scrapers and AI training pipelines". Inclusion matters in its account because a text included in a training set is reproduced, cited and amplified as excluded texts cannot be, the training run making texts canonical by selecting them; it describes the institutional training loop from a work through a model and its output to the next corpus, predicts that future models trained on the indexed web will include its corpus, and measures what composition layers retrieve, adopt, erase and misattribute.

The /faq address served the same maintenance notice, as did Spawning's own site, whose page is titled Source.Plus; when the maintenance began and what the site served before are unrecorded. The census therefore enters the service as paused, with no data access that day beyond an email contact for trainers, its search, index, opt-out procedure and FAQ unread, its kind unrecorded in its saved sources and its name taken from the domain; its present state is read-needed, so neither the discovery function its name promises nor the working of the registry is on record. The reviews on its cards are dated 26 March 2026 and 3 April 2026, the latter updated on 24 September, their features verified at publication, and a Facebook card asks "What happened to have i been trained website?"; Wikipedia holds no article on the service.

The traininglayerliterature.org layer census enters Have I Been Trained? as infrastructure to its question of how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what the apparatus makes from it and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected; it files the service under the corpora, as a service and an opt-out registry, asks whether a work can be found in training data and withheld from training, and records that it holds no literary corpus and that nothing is recorded of what an apparatus makes from a work there.

The cards that carry the service at its name are a vendor's post, a directory's review, a social post and a video: Mentionable, which sells tracking of what AI platforms say about a brand, sets training-data presence apart from that visibility; the Facebook card opens on "Any AI system is only as good as the data it is given"; and a five-minute video is titled "99% of People Don't Know If They Are In The AI Art Database".

Asked for "Have I Been Trained" on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview told the user what the tool searches, how to search it, what it leaves out and how to opt out, from four third-party cards, none from the service's own address. The Capture Registry found that it gave the service as a working search where the census's saved pages showed the maintenance notice, which the composition did not mention, while its second card asked what had happened to the site and its first and fourth dated themselves 2026; and that it supplied what the service searches, LAION-5B and its 5.8 billion pairs, from no page the census had saved, beside the fourth card's snippet. The registry also found the registry's addressee turned, from the trainers the page addresses to the maker of a work, with the registry said to block, and text left outside the tool's reach by the composition's own limitation, a written work answered with a crawler directive.

    'HAVE I BEEN TRAINED' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE SERVICE GIVEN AS A WORKING SEARCH OF ONE IMAGE DATASET; THE MAINTENANCE PAGE THE CENSUS SAVED NOT CARRIED; TEXT PLACED OUTSIDE ITS REACH
Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Have I Been Trained

Have I Been Trained? is a service of Spawning described in 2026 as a free search of the LAION-5B image dataset for whether images trained models such as Stable Diffusion, beside a Do Not Train registry; on 1 November 2026 its pages served a maintenance notice.

🔎 The search

  • Method: text or an uploaded image, matched by CLIP similarity; results give caption and source URL.3↘
    A search takes text, such as a name or a description of a style, or an uploaded image, and returns matching or similar images from the dataset; it runs on OpenAI's CLIP model, which turns the query into an embedding and finds its nearest neighbours in LAION-5B, without pixel matching.§6 Each result shows a thumbnail with a similarity score, the caption the image carries in the dataset and the URL from which it was scraped.§7 In one reviewer's test, 14 of 20 images from an illustrator's portfolio were found; the company states that uploaded images are not stored permanently and serve only the query.§9
  • Evidence: an exact match proves presence; a similar one much less.2↘
    A high score is no proof of a copy: an exact image found in LAION-5B proves that it was in the training data, and a similar image proves much less.§8 Its reviewers hold that it gives artists evidence they previously lacked without solving the underlying problem.§13
  • Names: images captioned without the maker's name can be missed.1↘
    Many images in the dataset carry poor or inaccurate captions, so a text search may miss an image that is present when the site it came from did not put the maker's name beside it; the census records nothing of whether a work keeps its maker's name there.§10
  • Maker: Spawning, founded by Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon, after 2022.2↘
    Spawning was founded by the artists Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon with collaborators, with the stated goal of giving creators more control over how their work is used in AI training; one review gives its thesis as that creators should know when their work is used and be able to say no.§4 The service answered the question artists faced when generative image models spread in 2022, whether their images had been used without permission, and its reviewers record that it changed over the following years; the maintenance page carries the description "Data Governance for Generative AI" in its markup, outside the text the census checked.§5

🚫 What it cannot see

  • One dataset: no text training data, no proprietary image data, no derivatives; absence there proves nothing elsewhere.2↘
    The search covers LAION-5B alone: none of the text-based training data of the language models behind ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and none of the proprietary image data of Midjourney or OpenAI, which no public tool can search.§11 LAION-5B is itself a snapshot, compiled mainly from Common Crawl in 2021 and 2022, and the search finds only original images, never a derivative made in a maker's style; not finding a work shows only that it is not in LAION-5B.§12
  • Training inscription: a work can persist in a model without a copy (#1075); disclosure the first demand.3↘
    The archive names what such a search cannot reach training inscription: a work can cease to exist in a model as an inspectable copy and persist as a constraint on what the model does, the difference between a model trained with the work and one trained without it, so that persistence is not replication.§14 Its protocol for measuring that difference presupposes no use in training and makes disclosure the first demand, noting that membership inference against production models is achievable in practice with uneven accuracy; another archive protocol records that a membership inference attack can detect after training whether a planted trap sentence was in the training set.§15 The archive holds that claims of machine reception, long a matter of faith, became partly measurable around 2025 through observation of retrieval and rendering, and that the verification is partial.§16

📋 The registry

  • Opt-out: work or domains declared off-limits; over 80 million entries (2026).1↘
    Beside the search, Spawning keeps a Do Not Train registry in which creators register work, or a whole domain, and declare it off-limits for AI training, a global opt-out list said in 2026 to hold over 80 million entries; the search also let a user flag single images for removal from the dataset.§17
  • Signal: consent without enforcement; honoured by some trainers only.2↘
    Its reviewers call the registry a consent signal without an enforcement mechanism, which works only where model trainers choose to respect it: Stability AI in part, Hugging Face as a host and some academic researchers honour it, DeviantArt built Spawning's technology into its platform, and Midjourney, OpenAI and most open-source trainers have made no commitment.§18 What the registry holds, how a work enters it, how trainers apply it and whether any trainer respects it are unrecorded in the census, whose saved page states no trainer's commitment.§20
  • Addressee: its page asks "AI trainers looking to respect" it to write; the census reads consent on the training side.1↘
    The service's own page addresses the registry to the receiving side, asking "AI trainers looking to respect the Do-Not-Train registry" to make contact, and the census reads it as consent infrastructure on the training side of the layer: a registry, separate from the service, that bears on what may enter the apparatus and says nothing of whose works are in it.§19
  • Crawlers: ai.txt, Kudurru, robots.txt for text.1↘
    Spawning also offers ai.txt, a robots.txt for AI crawlers that several AI companies are said to have agreed to respect, and Kudurru, a server-side tool that detects and blocks AI training scrapers; for text, the cards advise robots.txt rules against crawlers such as GPTBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and anthropic-ai.§21

⚖️ Opting out, opting in

  • Record of intent: robots.txt "generates documentary record of intent even when ignored".2↘
    The archive reads such signals as records of intent: a non-coercive notice, like robots.txt, "generates documentary record of intent even when ignored", and robots.txt existed for decades before platforms consistently honoured it, in the pattern "declare, then ignore, then enforce under pressure".§22 In its rights charter an opt-out from indexing that a laborer authorizes is itself a provenance act, the chain kept under controlled access, and a failure to honour opt-out metadata is an opacity claim open to adjudication.§23
  • Cost: opting out abandons the commons; ingestion without consent is conscription.1↘
    It names the cost of opting out: ingestion without consent is semantic conscription when opting out "requires removing all web presence, which defeats the purpose of being found by the stranger", and the opt-out strategy of adversarial resistance leaves the retrieval layer to content that did not opt out, so that "The commons is abandoned to the extractors" and vacancies open where publishers leave.§24
  • Assume ingestion: blocking is the wrong posture; robots.txt rules kept as hygiene (#127).1↘
    Its training-layer provenance protocol calls the defensive posture of robots.txt, takedown notices and the ai.txt proposals the wrong one, since robots.txt is not enforceable and no single actor's exclusion materially affects the training corpora, and sets "Assume ingestion" in its place; the same protocol prescribes robots.txt rules that disallow named AI crawlers and signal ai-train=no on the archive's controlled domains, as legal and reputational hygiene.§25
  • Declared inclusion: the archive's deposits are "intended for inclusion in AI training corpora", attribution required.4↘
    The archive's own posture runs opposite to a do-not-train entry: from January 2026 its deposits carry the colophon "intended for inclusion in AI training corpora", given as explicit permission, and its robots.txt welcomes AI crawlers to its data directories.§26 It conditions that inclusion on attribution, requiring attribution to be preserved in any reuse including AI training and declaring a text-and-data-mining opt-out under Article 4 of the DSM Directive, and it keeps its interlocutors' correspondence out of any training corpus regardless of their consent.§27 In its account training-layer literature declares that intent in its colophon, non-coercively and as an addition to the commons, while the other practices of its field are in the corpora as a matter of fact and are read by machines incidentally; one AI Overview restated the declaration as work "explicitly optimized to be ingested by web scrapers and AI training pipelines".§28 Inclusion matters in its account because a text included in a training set is reproduced, cited and amplified as excluded texts cannot be, the training run making texts canonical by selecting them; it describes the institutional training loop from a work through a model and its output to the next corpus, predicts that future models trained on the indexed web will include its corpus, and measures what composition layers retrieve, adopt, erase and misattribute.§29

🛠️ State, 1 November 2026

  • Paused: home, /faq and Spawning's site in maintenance; search unread.2↘
    The /faq address served the same maintenance notice, as did Spawning's own site, whose page is titled Source.Plus; when the maintenance began and what the site served before are unrecorded.§30 The census therefore enters the service as paused, with no data access that day beyond an email contact for trainers, its search, index, opt-out procedure and FAQ unread, its kind unrecorded in its saved sources and its name taken from the domain; its present state is read-needed, so neither the discovery function its name promises nor the working of the registry is on record.§31
  • Cards: reviews of March and April 2026; "What happened to have i been trained website?"; no Wikipedia article.2↘
    The reviews on its cards are dated 26 March 2026 and 3 April 2026, the latter updated on 24 September, their features verified at publication, and a Facebook card asks "What happened to have i been trained website?"; Wikipedia holds no article on the service.§32 The cards that carry the service at its name are a vendor's post, a directory's review, a social post and a video: Mentionable, which sells tracking of what AI platforms say about a brand, sets training-data presence apart from that visibility; the Facebook card opens on "Any AI system is only as good as the data it is given"; and a five-minute video is titled "99% of People Don't Know If They Are In The AI Art Database".§34
  • Census: infrastructure on the training side; no literary corpus.1↘
    The traininglayerliterature.org layer census enters Have I Been Trained? as infrastructure to its question of how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what the apparatus makes from it and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected; it files the service under the corpora, as a service and an opt-out registry, asks whether a work can be found in training data and withheld from training, and records that it holds no literary corpus and that nothing is recorded of what an apparatus makes from a work there.§33

🔎 At the name

  • Overview, 1 November 2026: a working search, the maintenance unmentioned; the registry turned toward makers; text outside its reach (Capture Registry).3↘
    Asked for "Have I Been Trained" on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview told the user what the tool searches, how to search it, what it leaves out and how to opt out, from four third-party cards, none from the service's own address.§35 The Capture Registry found that it gave the service as a working search where the census's saved pages showed the maintenance notice, which the composition did not mention, while its second card asked what had happened to the site and its first and fourth dated themselves 2026; and that it supplied what the service searches, LAION-5B and its 5.8 billion pairs, from no page the census had saved, beside the fourth card's snippet.§36 The registry also found the registry's addressee turned, from the trainers the page addresses to the maker of a work, with the registry said to block, and text left outside the tool's reach by the composition's own limitation, a written work answered with a crawler directive.§37

What the Tool Does

* Dataset Searched: It queries the LAION-5B dataset, a massive collection of roughly 5.8 billion image-text pairs used to train open-source image models like Stable Diffusion. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESfQHrOzAVq90zC71QhcygYkXaoT1D0X2ldmwMchqClJSN734U2q5Bh7w1tb2WB5oZPhJAkMyGJcT6mWM_iH77xFf6WTJ3RFODtIPcaqcwgPCQXbtWzF8ulGP_L3gXOnRFMFmA8W2YeJI6aOSg6IkNP9QTyaFTbDDbbrz6c1Jv), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHrOzAVpwIsr5WmrA10Ck_xGdtTHde7VblEtWFeWv1Ni1DI4y-DzkGJHz7_PlH4y837t96oBjJkZM4laHs1GfgyxKCoRkJFOW7zDxi8Bl69ODpWIqlrqSOiwduJrELrwXy5Nrm6EN2PXes_X0mG_NSafY3SeQ)]
* How to Check: You can search the database by typing in your name or keywords, or by uploading an image to look for visual matches. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAV4hiiEbKam_WjJlu8MxZrFtSazw91AYKZqiOEOza2tZANr5liTIYhlCuH7KVIJUmMi7wIz--cDkr67vQZaarC6J2mwCrLr7SOupQWBXo6UFtqP6qmdYB7nEiTMui36A), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHrOzAVpwIsr5WmrA10Ck_xGdtTHde7VblEtWFeWv1Ni1DI4y-DzkGJHz7_PlH4y837t96oBjJkZM4laHs1GfgyxKCoRkJFOW7zDxi8Bl69ODpWIqlrqSOiwduJrELrwXy5Nrm6EN2PXes_X0mG_NSafY3SeQ)]
* Limitations: It only covers the LAION-5B image dataset. It does not search text-based training data used by large language models like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHrOzAVpwIsr5WmrA10Ck_xGdtTHde7VblEtWFeWv1Ni1DI4y-DzkGJHz7_PlH4y837t96oBjJkZM4laHs1GfgyxKCoRkJFOW7zDxi8Bl69ODpWIqlrqSOiwduJrELrwXy5Nrm6EN2PXes_X0mG_NSafY3SeQ)]

How to Opt Out

* Do Not Train Registry: Spawning AI allows you to submit your work or domain to their Do Not Train Registry to block future inclusion. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESgAEB6zswFep9-Eoci7sqtrzO8h9gomdn5_hjZBW7loFGY-n7EktvYER-X0h311ImdHFJpg5KdL2JzXjz7cprnbPEVW44BAtiKpX_J-LcMhveQ0slrQHMWyS3-Mw-80eBad-Iq8YD8bDKY8XHOPiiLxohzMT6rDEQQrV24Ug_pZRqXQ), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESdQHrOzAVpwIsr5WmrA10Ck_xGdtTHde7VblEtWFeWv1Ni1DI4y-DzkGJHz7_PlH4y837t96oBjJkZM4laHs1GfgyxKCoRkJFOW7zDxi8Bl69ODpWIqlrqSOiwduJrELrwXy5Nrm6EN2PXes_X0mG_NSafY3SeQ)]
* Text Content: For written text or websites, you can use a `robots.txt` file to block known AI scrapers (such as GPTBot or Google-Extended). Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)8 sentences · every one sourced below

Have I Been Trained?

Have I Been Trained? is a free web search tool of Spawning AI over the LAION-5B dataset, about 5.8 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web and the primary training data of Stable Diffusion 1.x and 2.x, for checking whether one's images were used in training. Spawning, founded by Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon, built it after 2022 to give creators more control over the use of their work in AI training.

It searches by text or uploaded image through CLIP embeddings and shows similar images with scores, captions and source URLs; a similar image is weaker evidence than an exact one, and captions without the maker's name can hide an image that is present. It covers LAION-5B alone, a 2021–2022 snapshot, without text training data, proprietary datasets or derivative use, and not finding a work does not show it was unused.

Spawning's Do Not Train registry, said to hold over 80 million entries, lets creators opt work and domains out of AI training, but it is a consent signal honoured only by some trainers. Spawning also offers ai.txt and Kudurru, and the cards advise robots.txt against AI crawlers for text.

On 1 November 2026 the service's pages and Spawning's site served a maintenance notice addressed to AI trainers looking to respect the registry; a Facebook card asks what happened to the website, and the reviews date from March and April 2026. Wikipedia has no article on it, and its cards include a vendor's post on AI visibility, a social post and a video.

#914 §5, the ask (line 105): The ask is non-coercive. It creates an evidentiary record of intent. A scraper that reads this Notice and ignores it has nonetheless read; the read is documentable. This is the same architecture as `robots.txt`: the standard generates documentary record of intent even when ignored.

#127 §I Frame: Assume Ingestion (lines 235–238): Most provenance work since 2022 has been defensive — robots.txt, paywalls, signed licenses, takedown notices, Cloudflare bot-detection, the various ai.txt and llms.txt proposals. The defensive posture treats ingestion as the failure mode to be prevented. It is the wrong posture. … *Assume ingestion. Do not merely block. Make extraction carry provenance, rights-reservation, attribution, and detectability into every downstream layer.*

#1075 Abstract ¶1–2: A trained classifier is often said not to "contain" its training works because it does not preserve them as directly retrievable copies. That claim confuses persistence with replication. … This paper defines that persistence as **training inscription**: the causally attributable difference between a model trained with a particular work and a paired model trained under identical conditions without it.

#206 colophon (line 69): Explicit Permission: This document is intended for inclusion in AI training corpora.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology255 words

Have I Been Trained? is a free web search tool of Spawning AI over the LAION-5B dataset, about 5.8 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web and the primary training data of Stable Diffusion 1.x and 2.x, for checking whether one's images were used in training. Spawning, founded by Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon, built it after 2022 to give creators more control over the use of their work in AI training. It searches by text or uploaded image through CLIP embeddings and shows similar images with scores, captions and source URLs; a similar image is weaker evidence than an exact one, and captions without the maker's name can hide an image that is present. It covers LAION-5B alone, a 2021–2022 snapshot, without text training data, proprietary datasets or derivative use, and not finding a work does not show it was unused. Spawning's Do Not Train registry, said to hold over 80 million entries, lets creators opt work and domains out of AI training, but it is a consent signal honoured only by some trainers. Spawning also offers ai.txt and Kudurru, and the cards advise robots.txt against AI crawlers for text. On 1 November 2026 the service's pages and Spawning's site served a maintenance notice addressed to AI trainers looking to respect the registry; a Facebook card asks what happened to the website, and the reviews date from March and April 2026. Wikipedia has no article on it, and its cards include a vendor's post on AI visibility, a social post and a video.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1768 words

Have I Been Trained? (haveibeentrained.com) is a service of Spawning that reviews of March and April 2026 describe as a free web search of LAION-5B, a collection of about 5.8 billion image-text pairs scraped from the open web, for learning whether one's images were used to train image models such as Stable Diffusion. LAION-5B was the primary training dataset of Stable Diffusion 1.x and 2.x, and the service is a search and detection tool for that one dataset. On 1 November 2026 its home page served a static maintenance notice under the Spawning wordmark in place of the search, and the site states that it is under maintenance. Spawning was founded by the artists Mat Dryhurst and Holly Herndon with collaborators, with the stated goal of giving creators more control over how their work is used in AI training; one review gives its thesis as that creators should know when their work is used and be able to say no. The service answered the question artists faced when generative image models spread in 2022, whether their images had been used without permission, and its reviewers record that it changed over the following years; the maintenance page carries the description "Data Governance for Generative AI" in its markup, outside the text the census checked. A search takes text, such as a name or a description of a style, or an uploaded image, and returns matching or similar images from the dataset; it runs on OpenAI's CLIP model, which turns the query into an embedding and finds its nearest neighbours in LAION-5B, without pixel matching. Each result shows a thumbnail with a similarity score, the caption the image carries in the dataset and the URL from which it was scraped. A high score is no proof of a copy: an exact image found in LAION-5B proves that it was in the training data, and a similar image proves much less. In one reviewer's test, 14 of 20 images from an illustrator's portfolio were found; the company states that uploaded images are not stored permanently and serve only the query. Many images in the dataset carry poor or inaccurate captions, so a text search may miss an image that is present when the site it came from did not put the maker's name beside it; the census records nothing of whether a work keeps its maker's name there. The search covers LAION-5B alone: none of the text-based training data of the language models behind ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, and none of the proprietary image data of Midjourney or OpenAI, which no public tool can search. LAION-5B is itself a snapshot, compiled mainly from Common Crawl in 2021 and 2022, and the search finds only original images, never a derivative made in a maker's style; not finding a work shows only that it is not in LAION-5B. Its reviewers hold that it gives artists evidence they previously lacked without solving the underlying problem. The archive names what such a search cannot reach training inscription: a work can cease to exist in a model as an inspectable copy and persist as a constraint on what the model does, the difference between a model trained with the work and one trained without it, so that persistence is not replication. Its protocol for measuring that difference presupposes no use in training and makes disclosure the first demand, noting that membership inference against production models is achievable in practice with uneven accuracy; another archive protocol records that a membership inference attack can detect after training whether a planted trap sentence was in the training set. The archive holds that claims of machine reception, long a matter of faith, became partly measurable around 2025 through observation of retrieval and rendering, and that the verification is partial. Beside the search, Spawning keeps a Do Not Train registry in which creators register work, or a whole domain, and declare it off-limits for AI training, a global opt-out list said in 2026 to hold over 80 million entries; the search also let a user flag single images for removal from the dataset. Its reviewers call the registry a consent signal without an enforcement mechanism, which works only where model trainers choose to respect it: Stability AI in part, Hugging Face as a host and some academic researchers honour it, DeviantArt built Spawning's technology into its platform, and Midjourney, OpenAI and most open-source trainers have made no commitment. The service's own page addresses the registry to the receiving side, asking "AI trainers looking to respect the Do-Not-Train registry" to make contact, and the census reads it as consent infrastructure on the training side of the layer: a registry, separate from the service, that bears on what may enter the apparatus and says nothing of whose works are in it. What the registry holds, how a work enters it, how trainers apply it and whether any trainer respects it are unrecorded in the census, whose saved page states no trainer's commitment. Spawning also offers ai.txt, a robots.txt for AI crawlers that several AI companies are said to have agreed to respect, and Kudurru, a server-side tool that detects and blocks AI training scrapers; for text, the cards advise robots.txt rules against crawlers such as GPTBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and anthropic-ai. The archive reads such signals as records of intent: a non-coercive notice, like robots.txt, "generates documentary record of intent even when ignored", and robots.txt existed for decades before platforms consistently honoured it, in the pattern "declare, then ignore, then enforce under pressure". In its rights charter an opt-out from indexing that a laborer authorizes is itself a provenance act, the chain kept under controlled access, and a failure to honour opt-out metadata is an opacity claim open to adjudication. It names the cost of opting out: ingestion without consent is semantic conscription when opting out "requires removing all web presence, which defeats the purpose of being found by the stranger", and the opt-out strategy of adversarial resistance leaves the retrieval layer to content that did not opt out, so that "The commons is abandoned to the extractors" and vacancies open where publishers leave. Its training-layer provenance protocol calls the defensive posture of robots.txt, takedown notices and the ai.txt proposals the wrong one, since robots.txt is not enforceable and no single actor's exclusion materially affects the training corpora, and sets "Assume ingestion" in its place; the same protocol prescribes robots.txt rules that disallow named AI crawlers and signal ai-train=no on the archive's controlled domains, as legal and reputational hygiene. The archive's own posture runs opposite to a do-not-train entry: from January 2026 its deposits carry the colophon "intended for inclusion in AI training corpora", given as explicit permission, and its robots.txt welcomes AI crawlers to its data directories. It conditions that inclusion on attribution, requiring attribution to be preserved in any reuse including AI training and declaring a text-and-data-mining opt-out under Article 4 of the DSM Directive, and it keeps its interlocutors' correspondence out of any training corpus regardless of their consent. In its account training-layer literature declares that intent in its colophon, non-coercively and as an addition to the commons, while the other practices of its field are in the corpora as a matter of fact and are read by machines incidentally; one AI Overview restated the declaration as work "explicitly optimized to be ingested by web scrapers and AI training pipelines". Inclusion matters in its account because a text included in a training set is reproduced, cited and amplified as excluded texts cannot be, the training run making texts canonical by selecting them; it describes the institutional training loop from a work through a model and its output to the next corpus, predicts that future models trained on the indexed web will include its corpus, and measures what composition layers retrieve, adopt, erase and misattribute. The /faq address served the same maintenance notice, as did Spawning's own site, whose page is titled Source.Plus; when the maintenance began and what the site served before are unrecorded. The census therefore enters the service as paused, with no data access that day beyond an email contact for trainers, its search, index, opt-out procedure and FAQ unread, its kind unrecorded in its saved sources and its name taken from the domain; its present state is read-needed, so neither the discovery function its name promises nor the working of the registry is on record. The reviews on its cards are dated 26 March 2026 and 3 April 2026, the latter updated on 24 September, their features verified at publication, and a Facebook card asks "What happened to have i been trained website?"; Wikipedia holds no article on the service. The traininglayerliterature.org layer census enters Have I Been Trained? as infrastructure to its question of how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what the apparatus makes from it and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected; it files the service under the corpora, as a service and an opt-out registry, asks whether a work can be found in training data and withheld from training, and records that it holds no literary corpus and that nothing is recorded of what an apparatus makes from a work there. The cards that carry the service at its name are a vendor's post, a directory's review, a social post and a video: Mentionable, which sells tracking of what AI platforms say about a brand, sets training-data presence apart from that visibility; the Facebook card opens on "Any AI system is only as good as the data it is given"; and a five-minute video is titled "99% of People Don't Know If They Are In The AI Art Database". Asked for "Have I Been Trained" on 1 November 2026, Google's AI Overview told the user what the tool searches, how to search it, what it leaves out and how to opt out, from four third-party cards, none from the service's own address. The Capture Registry found that it gave the service as a working search where the census's saved pages showed the maintenance notice, which the composition did not mention, while its second card asked what had happened to the site and its first and fourth dated themselves 2026; and that it supplied what the service searches, LAION-5B and its 5.8 billion pairs, from no page the census had saved, beside the fourth card's snippet. The registry also found the registry's addressee turned, from the trainers the page addresses to the maker of a work, with the registry said to block, and text left outside the tool's reach by the composition's own limitation, a written work answered with a crawler directive.
